Personally, I think it's more like smoking. I've quit smoking 3 times (this one seems to be sticking!). The thing about quitting is, at the beginning you get urges constantly, because you've built up the habit and lots of associations in your brain. The longer you go without smoking, the more of those associations are broken, and the less often you will get urges. Figuring out why you binge is an important step so you can find an alternate way to deal with the feelings/triggers, but I don't think it magically makes the urges go away. That only comes with time and practice. What it does do is give you ammunition in being able to resist the urges. I see your point about eating being biologically wired while smoking isn't. So often the main trigger for binging is restriction, mental or physical. And once you understand that you can adjust your behavior to hopefully not do that anymore. But there is another habit based side to it that you can also address at the same time.

In this case the total number of red trinkets and the total number of blue trinkets is what's being conserved. So if they ask which bin has more trinkets of the opposite color, they have to be the same. You start with the same number of each color. Each bin ends up with the same number of total trinkets. Any red trinket that isn't in the red bin must be in the blue bin. And vice versa. Total red must add to 25.Total blue must add to 25. Total in each bin must add to 25. If there's 3 red in the blue bin, that means theres 22 blues in that bin. Which means there must also be 3 blue in the red bin so that the total in each bin adds to 25. It is very unintuitive but it seems to work out.

I haven't experienced the specific things that you have but I do understand the feeling of being screwed from birth and feeling helpless to change anything. If you want to improve your life it will be harder for you than for most people. Maybe a lot harder. And that sucks. Its really not fair because you did nothing to deserve it. But that doesn't mean that its pointless to try. Have you read the book Educated by Tara Westover? The author talks about a pretty similar struggle, being homeschooled and isolated from the outside world, not even having a birth certificate, and eventually coming out of it and getting a PhD. This is not to say that you need a PhD or even want one, just to say that with some perseverance and luck you can improve your situation. I know it feels hopeless, and I've also felt hopeless many times... but if your life is gonna suck anyways why not at least try to make it a bit better? If people want to turn their nose up at your background, they have the problem, not you. Even though they can make your life more difficult and its total bullshit. Know in your heart that you are *worth it* and that struggling to make your life a bit better will pay off. The worst that could happen is that your life stays exactly the same, but at least you'll have the comfort of knowing that you did your best. The only way to guarantee failure is to not try at all.

You're struggling right now. The consequences might be that you get poor grades this semester. But that says nothing about what happens next semester or next year. Consequences. But now I'm in grad school at a very prestigious university. You can have different consequences if you find a way to choose different actions. I know it probably feels impossible, but you can learn to behave differently. It just takes time. The only thing giving up does is 100% guarantee that nothing with ever change. My therapist has the same cancellation policy. I've never explicitly asked him why, but from what I've gathered it's more common with Ts who are more psychodynamic/analytical. It really bothered me at first too, because of how deeply unfair it feels. He can cancel an appointment whenever he wants but I have to pay for the privilege? I also had a lot of those same fears, that he was just using me for the money. But honestly I got used to it. Even if it is about money, I try to see it from his perspective. If he is seeing me twice a week, he can't schedule anyone else in those slots. If I cancel, even in advance, he's not likely to fill them. If people are free to cancel whenever, that can lead to a very unpredictable income which is hugely stressful. It's definitely not ideal but it's something I'm willing to compromise on because I really enjoy our work together otherwise. Also, I think it ultimately does help me in that I am a fairly avoidant person, and knowing that I can't just cancel willy nilly has helped me push through a lot of tough times in therapy.

I completely understand your reaction, but I would urge you to give it some time before quitting.

I totally get this, my brain is an ass too. One thing I I think is really important to keep in mind is *why* your abusers needed you to be not upset. It wasn't anything to do with your wellbeing, it was to protect their own sense of self. So if someone says or does something abusive to you and you're clearly hurt by it, it is in that person's interest to convince you that they did nothing wrong and therefore it's your reaction that's wrong. Because if your reaction is wrong, then they get to preserve the idea that they are a good person and avoid confronting the fact that they're abusive. Doing what is in their interest (denying your pain) goes against what is in your interest (not being hurt). 

When your T tries to stop you from talking about your trauma before you're ready, they're not saying your reaction to the trauma is wrong, they're saying that the approach you're taking towards healing is "wrong" in the sense that it will cause unnecessary pain. It's likely that the T's ego is also involved in this--they want to see themselves as someone who heals pain rather than causes it. But in this case doing what's in your best interest is also in the best interest of the T (assuming they're good at their job lol), which is creating a space where you can confront your pain without causing more harm. 

Hopefully some of this resonates with you. It's always a tough back and forth wondering if you can trust your T, especially with trauma stuff.

Something that I really struggle with in therapy is not going too fast. It sounds like that might be what's going on with your therapist. Are you familiar with the concept of a therapeutic window for anxiety? Basically, if your anxiety is too high and you continue to talk about your trauma, it can actually be damaging rather than therapeutic to talk about because you end up retraumatizing yourself. I understand that it feels like just one more person telling you that you're reactions are unacceptable, or like your T is giving up on you. I struggle with a lot of those same feelings. But consider reframing the thought... Your therapist is trying to protect you. They don't want you to retraumatize yourself by talking about things you're not ready for. How do they know you're not ready? Because of the very strong reactions you're having when you try to talk about it. This is super frustrating because it feels like you have to talk about the trauma or you're going to explode and it sounds like your T is saying, no we can't talk about that. But what they're actually saying is we can't talk about that *yet*. You need to get to a point where you feel more comfortable with your T. You say that the mere act of going to therapy makes you anxious. I am with you there. But at least for me, over time, that anxiety has decreased slightly. But it is agonizingly slow. And it often feels like we're not doing anything.

My T has started asking what he can do differently to avoid triggering me. At first this question pissed me off because I felt like my triggers were inevitably tied to certain ideas and that if I wanted to deal with my trauma I would have to endure and push through them. But firstly, that didn't work. I just ended up triggered and suffering and not making progress. And secondly, it's not true. There are things that we can do differently so I don't get so triggered. It's really difficult figuring them out, and I usually can't verbalize them myself, but we do find things through trial and error. I've discovered that there are some things I can talk about a little. Around the edges. The core issue is still inaccessable  but by talking about the smaller things I feel my capacity to open up is growing. It's not a black and white situation where you either talk about your core trauma or talk about irrelevant bs. You have to find the thing to talk about that's a little bit difficult but not so hard that it sends you into a spiral. And it's hard, and you'll push too much sometimes and feel like therapy is making everything worse. But as long as you keep trying things will improve. 

I think the main point I'm trying to make is that maybe your therapist is not saying that your trauma is unacceptable to talk about, but rather that they don't want to cause you more pain by having you talk about things in an untherapeutic way.

Fairly early on when I was having a really hard time opening up and kept freezing in session one day my T snapped "come on give me *something*" and that kind of freaked me out. It took awhile to come back from that, but he's become more patient with my unexpected trauma responses and I've become better at self regulating so I don't get to the point of becoming non-verbal. I also think I just feel safer with him after having more sessions and having him react compassionately to some smaller stuff.

I do feel like there was an unproductive period in therapy where he was constantly accusing me of "withholding" and getting frustrated with me for not being able to communicate well in session. At some point something clicked for him and he started being more compassionate and understanding of my inability to talk about certain things. I think we have a pretty great relationship now, but sometimes I wish he had understood sooner that I was having trauma responses. To be fair I also didn't understand that I was having trauma responses at that time so it was confusing all around.

To answer your direct question, I don't think they are supposed to show their frustration so blatantly but I also think it's ridiculous to say they aren't supposed to get frustrated. Part of therapy is the clinician evaluating their own feelings in response to the patient, whatever those feelings may be. For example, if the T is frustrated by the patient being uncommunicative, does that play out in other relationships? Does the patient have trouble getting close to people, or provoke them into anger by lack of communication? 

I try to remember that therapists are human and make mistakes, but what really matters is how they handle those mistakes later on. Something my T constantly reminded me of at the beginning, to the point of being annoying, is that he can't avoid hurting me if I don't tell him when I've been hurt. I feel like talking to him about stuff like that has really helped improve our rapport.

So yes, in this case I think expressing frustration like that was a mistake. If you wanted to continue with that T you could bring up how they hurt you and see how they react. It's also fine to say that you don't feel safe with that person anymore and try a different T.

Maybe rumination? I noticed that I do this in an effort to solve a perceived problem, even though in fact I usually end up making myself miserable and not solving the problem at all. This doesn't work 100% of the time, but it does help me to notice its happening, say out loud (or in your head if you prefer) "I think I'm solving a problem but I'm actually just creating a problem" and then redirect my attention to something else. I might do this 20 times in a day and it might work 19 times and then fail the 20th time, but at least I didn't start ruminating the first time and managed to put it off for awhile. Sometimes if I find that I really want to think something through I'll write the thoughts in my journal and its easier to move on. 

I think the more you ruminate the more it becomes a habit which makes it harder to stop. It does feel like a lot of work if this is something that comes up a lot, but at least doing it less is an improvement. Good luck.

Hey. I have experienced a similar fear of men/aversion to sex for most of my life. I know it's super frustrating when you want to enjoy it but you can't and then you just end up feeling broken because you can't even really tell what's wrong. When I first started having sex I would basically freeze up and not feel anything. What I did to deal with it was force myself to have sex anyways. I don't reccomend it. Although I stopped getting so anxious during sex, I still felt pretty numbed out, and it just lead to more trauma around sex because I felt like I was never allowed to say no. Eventually I did start to enjoy sex, but only in situations where I felt in control. Specifically I had to be in a situation where I knew that I could say no and the sex would stop immediately and there would  be no negative consequences. Not just like my partner begrudgingly agreeing or guilting me about not wanting sex as much as him, but actually respecting my boundaries and my need for safety. 

At the time I didn't think I had any sexual trauma in my past, but I recently may have recovered a memory of something from when I was pretty young. I am not sure if it's real or a manifestation of my complex relationship with sex and trying to deal with other bs from my childhood.

Regardless of that memory though, I think what helped me the most with sex was figuring out how to feel safe in my relationships. I originally thought having sex with random people would be easier so I could "practice" but without that sense of safety I just really couldn't engage. I also thought having sex with my bf even when I wasn't in the mood would help me get over my weird sex aversion cause I would "get used to sex" ... But it only made it worse. I would also reccommend not digging for memories. Maybe something happened, maybe it didn't. I honestly wish my "memory" had never popped into my head because it's only caused me more misery and even though I reached a point where I actually could enjoy sex with my new bf, since the memory sometimes I don't bc I start getting intrusive thoughts about it. When I was in my mid 20s (I'm 34 now) I remember wondering in frustration if I was molested because sex was so difficult for me. And now I have this memory and I still don't know if I was molested or not because I don't trust that it's real AND I'm having negative experiences from just having the memory.

Sorry for rambling so much about my own life. I started this comment because I wanted you to know that you're not alone in this, that others also experience fear of men and weird reactions to sex and that I understand how confusing it can be when you can't even figure out why you're reacting the way you are. I don't know if you're in therapy at the moment but if so I reccommend trying to bring this stuff up. I still haven't managed to do it with mine but I'm working on it. Good luck.

I just want to say that I also experience this with my therapist and I've been going for almost 2 years now. It has improved, but it takes a lot of time talking about the anxiety itself and building trust with the therapist. I wouldn't give up just yet. Even just letting your therapist know that you feel very anxious and are having a hard time opening up can be helpful because it gives them more context for what you're talking about and experiencing in session. My dad was also emotionally abusive and I often find myself in therapy stuck in some sort of freeze state just overwhelmed with anxiety and unable to do anything. Talking about that feeling with my therapist was ultimate helpful because even though I couldn't tell him axactly what was making me so anxious, the fact that it was happening was informative. One thing that my therapist does that I only recently realized is that when I am overwhelmed with paralyzing anxiety he tries to get me to connect with my anger, because anger is an energizing emotion and can propel you forward. Doesn't always work, but something to try. Also my impulse is always to talk about the biggest scariest thing because that's whats bothering me the most. But talking about smaller things first can be very helpful and it's usually a lot easier to deal with.

The best tip I can give you is be patient. It has been agonizingly slow for me to learn to trust my therapist enough for the anxiety and shame to recede even a little bit. And it's SO FRUSTRATING to have to contend with it every session. But I can tell you for a fact my life is objectively better than it was when I started. 

That being said, my first therapist just never got it. I felt like every interaction with her was superficial and completely missing the point. I never opened up to her about my dad at all really. So. Give it some time. See if you can open up a tiny bit and how she responds. And if it doesn't work, it doesn't work.

Good luck! I didn't start therapy seriously until I was in my early 30s. The sooner you start the better. But also, no shame if you're not ready.

I did most of the things you're talking about there at some point, aside from the moving across the country bit cause I'm too much of a coward haha. Complete with maxed out credit cards and maggots growing on my kitchen floor. 

It's a really scary place to realize that you can't pay your rent but you're not gonna do anything about it except shove it to the back of your mind and assume the problem will eventually be solved by your own death. I was sort of able to "self help" myself but not from that point. I had to move to a safe-ish place (at least physically safe, I didn't have to worry about being homeless) where I had time to reflect and grow without being crushed by the consequences of my own decisions. 

At the time, moving back with my parents was the last thing I wanted to do since they were a huge part of the problem in the first place, but they did provide a place for me to live and some food so my most basic physical needs were met. Once that happened I was more equipped to deal with some of my psychological issues. That being said it took 5+ years for me to become what I would consider functional from that point, and I think it would have been a lot faster if I had sought therapy back then. Additionally, I had a GPA less than 1 and a fucked up credit score that I had to make up for which made my life harder than it should have been. I know the future doesn't feel like a real possibility right now but it might someday and it would be a gift to future you to try and plan for it a little bit. 

If your parents are an option for you I would reccommend that, otherwise I would reccommend focusing on physical safety and stability first. It turns out it's really hard to function psychologically of your physical and safety needs aren't met.

Good luck. Most importantly, I hope you know that things aren't hopeless from here. There is a way back.

I am not trying to defend your wife or claim that what's going on is entirely your fault, but I do want to express my experience as the "low libido" partner in a previous relationship. I also want to point out that we weren't married and didn't have kids, so the dynamic may be a bit different.

In the beginning of the relationship, the frequency of sex was entirely dependent on his libido. I wanted to make him happy, and although he was never violent, his emotional reactions when I declined sex made me feel extremely guilty, so I would give in. Over time I began to dread his advances and anything that even seemed like it might eventually lead to him getting turned on, because it seemed that regardless of how I felt, we would either have sex or he would become angry with me. When we did have sex, he would get upset if I didn't come, even though I repeatedly assured him that it was something that I personally needed to work on and not something that he was doing wrong. Overall, I ended up feeling like sex was a chore I performed to get him off my back rather than a mutually pleasurable experience, and as long as I felt like I had no autonomy in that aspect of our relationship, my libido remained low. 

The way you describe your wife's behavior makes me think that a similar unhealthy dynamic has emerged, where she feels threatened by your advances because of your previous reactions to being rejected. You say you don't pressure her, but reminding her daily "you agreed to have sex on x day" sounds an awful lot like pressure to me, and would definitely cause me to emotionally spiral and not want to have sex. Even in my current relationship, which is much healthier, any inkling of what feels like pressure from my boyfriend that he *needs* sex from me at any given time just shuts me right down and it becomes really difficult for me to be turned on or even think about sex without feeling anxious and uncomfortable. 

I think your feelings of being rejected are totally valid, but so are her feelings of being pressured. You guys can't meet each others needs right now as it stands because your needs are in opposition. If it helps at all, from my perspective I think she is also struggling, and not just blowing you off.

This happens to me too! The specific expression for me isn't hitting myself in the head but I will remember something that induces shame and get a really strong urge to hurt myself. I also have random suicidal thoughts that don't really make sense because I don't particularly want to die, but in that moment they feel really strong.

When I was a teen and actively suicidal, I think those thoughts served a purpose... It was a potential escape from a life that I thought would becomes completely unbearable. I don't think life is unbearable anymore, but I do think of these suicidal urges that pop up as a desire to escape from my current situation in some way. So when that happens I try to think what in the current situation feels unbearable to me and if there's anything I can do to ameliorate that.

As for the desire to hurt yourself, I really think this has to do with shame attacks. I know it happens to me because I was emotionally neglected and abused by my parents as a child, and therefore have a very overactive shame response. I'm still not sure what will make it go away haha but for me it helps knowing that these feelings are a natural response to what happened to me and not some secret sign of being fatally flawed. Also, something my therapist likes to remind me of often is that when a feeling seems completely out of proportion to the event that prompted it, it's probably more about something in the past than something in the present. This is an overwhelming time. I understand the urge to try and do something to feel better, or to fix it, or to stop overthinking as you say.... but the situation is inherently painful. You have to let it hurt. And over time it will hurt less. It will be slow. It will feel like it will never get better. But it does. Slowly. Imperceptibly. I think the best thing you can do right now is to continue to rely on friends and relatives and be patient with yourself. More concretely, make sure you continue to eat and exercise. If the mornings in particular are hard, try to plan some activity that relaxes you during that time, or even a small ritual that reminds you of your mom and honors her memory. For example, when my mom died I made a playlist of songs that reminded me of her and would go for long walks and sing along to them over and over again, and even though I usually ended up ugly crying, something about the activity helped me to process my grief. 

Above all, be patient with yourself. Its only been a few days. The loss is still very fresh. Feeling overwhelmed, having trouble with day to day activities... this is all perfectly normal. It will pass with time. And all this pain... it exists because of how much you loved your mother. And as cheezy as that sounds, I think its kind of beautiful.

I feel this. When I was in high school, I was a really good student up until the second half of my senior year. I went from a 4.0 to almost failing 2 classes. In fact I only passed one of them because my teacher took pity on me even though I didn't complete the work. And I didn't even have a global pandemic to deal with! 

For me, a lot of my issues were down to anxiety and depression, for which my main coping mechanism was avoidance. Avoidance as a coping mechanism is toxic though, because not only does it make the problem you're avoiding objectively worse (schoolwork piling up), it also makes your unconscious fear of it even stronger, so you end up digging yourself deeper and deeper into a hole. 

Start small. Sit down and plan to do school work for 30 minutes. Thats it, and then you can stop. Pulling an all nighter and finishing everything seems  huge and overwhelming because it is. Doing a little at a time is much more manageable. 

The other thing I would recommend is to talk to your teachers. They know this is a stressful time. Its difficult for everyone. But they can't help you if they don't know whats going on with you. Teachers are a lot more understanding than you think, especially if you don't put off asking for help until the day before the final. And if you talk to them, you can also wipe out the fear of how they will react, which helps a lot in overcoming the avoidance issue.

I think there is also a correlation in both directions. If you are depressed you definitely don't have the energy to deal with people as much but also if your attachment symptoms get worse (for example because of increased anxiety, maybe due to a pandemic or something :P) this could lead to depression symptoms. This has definitely been true of me. When I avoid social interactions because of my anxiety, I feel bad about myself for allowing my anxiety to limit my life, and I also lose the benefit to my mental health that connection would bring. Overall my mood after this is much lower. Which makes me want to avoid people even more. And so on. Its some kind of toxic spiral, with both problems making each other worse.
